newsitem.title: FRANCE: France sends six light tanks to Congo.
newsitem.headline: France sends six light tanks to Congo.

text.p: Light tanks began arriving in Brazzaville on Thursday to reinforce 1,250 French soldiers evacuating foreigners from the embattled Congolese capital, the army said on Thursday.
A French soldier was wounded by firing around Brazzaville airport but his life was not in danger.
A French junior minister meanwhile said he had unconfirmed reports that thousands of civilians may have been killed in the week-old fighting but Paris had no way of checking the number of casualties.
"The first of six ERC-90 Sagaies from the Foreign Legion's First Cavalry Regiment has arrived by plane," a military spokesman said. "We expect all six to be there imminently," he said.
The Sagaie, designed for desert warfare, carries a 90 mm cannon and used in reconnaissance units of armoured divisions.

The tanks will give added firepower to French troops whose mission to protect and evacuate foreign nationals from bitter fighting between supporters of President Pascal Lissouba and those of former Marxist military leader Denis Sassou Nguesso.
The EBR armoured cars used by the 1,250 foreign legionnaires and marine paratroopers for forays into the city to rescue civilians only have machine guns.

Secretary of State for Economic Cooperation Charles Josselin told the newspaper Le Monde that witnesses had spoken of several thousand dead, but French military specialists dismissed talk of such high casualty figures in a week of fighting.

"We don't have the means to evaluate how many civilians have been killed, but some witnesses speak of thousands," Josselin said, adding that French troops would not intervene to separate the warring sides.

A radio report on Wednesday had quoted an evacuee as saying French soldiers on the spot had told him there might be 10,000 dead, but military sources in Paris said they had no such figures and were wary of them.

"We don't know how many have been killed. Because much of Brazzaville is made up of shantytowns where people live tightly packed, it is possible some rounds from multiple rockets launchers they are using may have caused heavy casualties in places," one senior officer told Reuters in Paris:
"There could be 200 dead or 1,000 dead in the very worst case scenario but we don't know," he said.
The French army has rescued and brought to Brazzaville airport 2,954 people of 50 nationalities, the army said.

Of these, 2,507 have been flown out, mostly to Gabon, aboard French air force C-130 Hercules and C-160 Transalls in what the army described as "very difficult conditions". The evacuees included 1,282 French nationals.
The planes have been taking off and landing on an airstrip around which rival factions have clashed. The area where the evacuees gathered came under fire on Wednesday.
Reports from Brazzaville said mortar blasts and grenade explosions echoed around areas near the airport early on Thursday despite a ceasefire called to end a week of fighting.
Brazzaville itself saw quiet after Lissouba ordered his troops to stop firing on Wednesday afternoon and Sassou Nguesso urged his supporters to observe the ceasefire.
The clashes began on June 5 after soldiers surrounded Sassou Nguesso's home as part of a crackdown on militias and illegal arms ahead of a July 27 presidential election.
Lissouba won a 1992 presidential election after Sassou Nguesso, president from 1979, bowed to calls for multi-party politics.
